questions.q: Why does sharing-model design usually involve weighing trade-offs rather than finding the one correct answer?
options: Salesforce only supports one sharing mechanism per object, so there's nothing to compare
Most real requirements can be satisfied by more than one combination of sharing tools, each with a different cost profile
Trade-off analysis is only relevant for Experience Cloud sites, not internal sharing
Because sharing rules always outperform role hierarchy, so the choice is rarely close
questions.explain: Nearly any real requirement can be satisfied by several different sharing designs; the work is choosing among options that all technically work, not finding the single one that does.

questions.q: In the field-service scenario (400 technicians, 30 regions, reassigned quarterly), what made Territory Management the recommended option over a one-role-per-region hierarchy?
options: The requirement was territory-shaped and changed on a predictable, frequent cadence, which Territory Management's Planning state is specifically built to absorb
Territory Management has no build cost at all
Role hierarchy cannot technically restrict access by region under any configuration
Public groups and sharing rules were ruled out entirely for this object
questions.explain: The recommendation hinged on the requirement's shape and change frequency — a frequently-reassigned geographic axis is exactly what Enterprise Territory Management, with its Planning-state validation step, is purpose-built to handle.

questions.q: Which dimension specifically asks whether a reviewer can open Setup and see why a user has access, without reading Apex code?
options: Build cost
Maintenance cost
Auditability and transparency
Flexibility for future change
questions.explain: Auditability and transparency is about whether access decisions are traceable declaratively (as covered in Lesson 21's audit tools) versus buried in code only a developer can follow.

questions.q: What is the main maintenance risk of the one-role-per-region option (Option A) in the worked scenario?
options: It is not declarative, so every change requires a code deployment
It cannot be audited through Setup at all
It would violate the per-object Restriction Rule limit
Quarterly region reassignment requires re-parenting or reassigning roles for a large share of 400 users, each change triggering sharing recalculation
questions.explain: Role hierarchy wasn't designed to double as a frequently-changing region map; each quarterly reassignment creates a heavy maintenance and recalculation burden at this scale.

questions.q: A good trade-off recommendation, as this lesson frames it, should primarily do what?
options: Name the winning option only, trusting the reader to infer the reasoning
Explain the specific reasoning — tied to the requirement's own shape and cadence — for why one option fits better than the alternatives
Avoid naming a winner at all, since all options are equally valid
Default to whichever option has the lowest build cost, regardless of other factors
questions.explain: A recommendation should name the reasoning explicitly and tie it to facts about the requirement itself, since the same recommendation could be wrong under a different cadence or scale.
